new_slides.title: Flight starts when net drive crosses threshold
body: A **threshold** is the level of excitation a network must reach before it switches from rest to its active state. Inputs that start flight differ in sign: head wind adds excitation, whereas tarsal contact subtracts it, so a locust standing in wind can stay grounded while its feet hold the network below threshold.

Removing contact and adding wind act on the same balance from opposite sides. Release takes away inhibition and frees existing drive operate, while wind supplies new drive; either change can carry the network across threshold, after which the network produces its own rhythm.

The 404 interneurons are a candidate site for this sum. Wind and dimming both raise their tonic firing, and a burst at the kick adds more, so a jump can combine lost contact with central excitation and open the wings sooner than any single tested route.

figure.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 2. Tarsal-release and wing-opening records.

transcript: Slides 2, 5 and 6 compare three ways flight can begin, each with its own latency. Treating them as inputs to one threshold explains why such different stimuli all start the same motor program.
Inputs of opposite sign.
Camhi found that contact under the feet can inhibit flight in a tethered animal, while wind on the head hairs releases it.
An inhibitory input and an excitatory input can be combined on one scale, the net drive reaching the flight circuit.
Release versus drive.
Lowering the rod adds nothing new; it removes a brake, and the flight network can then respond to whatever excitation is already present.
Wind works the other way, by adding excitation until the circuit switches on, and in both cases the rhythm itself comes from the thoracic network.
Where the inputs could meet.
Pearson and colleagues found that 404 neurons fire tonically during flight released by wind or by sudden darkness, and burst at the moment a kick is triggered.

A jump removes ground contact and, if the kick-related burst also occurs, adds central drive at the same time, which could explain why wing opening in free jumps outpaces both the wind reflex and tarsal release.
refs: J. M. Camhi (1969c). Locust wind receptors. III. Contribution to flight initiation and lift control. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):363–373. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.363
K. G. Pearson; D. N. Reye; D. W. Parsons; G. Bicker (1985). Flight-initiating interneurons in the locust. Journal of Neurophysiology 53(4):910–925. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.1985.53.4.910

new_slides.title: Socket pivot converts wind into receptor spikes
body: **Mechanotransduction** is the conversion of a mechanical force into an electrical signal. Wind pushes the curved shaft, the shaft pivots in its socket, and its base moves the dendrite attached off-center near the pivot. That movement deforms the dendritic membrane and opens mechanically gated ion channels.

Cations flowing through those channels depolarize the dendrite, producing a **receptor potential** graded with deflection. Once that potential passes spike threshold, the axon fires at a rate that rises with depolarization, so larger deflections give higher spike rates.

Adaptation then reshapes the rate over time. The fast decline in the first half-second leaves a strong onset burst followed by a lower maintained rate, so one receptor feeds two kinds of interneuron: sustained wind-indicator cells read the maintained rate, and acceleration cells respond most to rapid onset.

figure.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 2. Sensory spikes during airflow onset and cessation.

transcript: Slides 7 to 10 describe the hair, its socket and its spike output without walking through the steps that link wind to spikes. Those steps are general features of insect mechanoreceptors applied to this hair.
From airflow to membrane.
The shaft does not bend along its length; it rotates at the socket, so the base acts like a lever on the eccentric dendrite.
Deforming the dendrite membrane opens channels that respond to mechanical force, the first electrical event in the pathway.
From membrane to spikes.
The inward current makes a graded depolarization, and the spike-initiating zone converts it into a spike rate.
Camhi’s maximum rate near 200 spikes per second at onset therefore reflects both a large deflection and a fresh, unadapted receptor.
Two signals from one receptor.
The onset burst and the maintained rate carry different information, and Camhi’s interneuron classes appear to emphasize one or the other.
Wind-indicator cells kept firing in steady wind, while acceleration cells were strongly driven only by fast increases in airflow.
refs: J. M. Camhi (1969a). Locust wind receptors. I. Transducer mechanics and sensory response. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):335–348. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.335
J. M. Camhi (1969b). Locust wind receptors. II. Interneurones in the cervical connective. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):349–362. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.349

extra_figures.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 1. Seta shaft, socket and attached sensory cell.

new_slides.title: Axon diameter sets how fast wind news travels
body: **Conduction velocity** is the speed at which an action potential travels along an axon. Each spike spreads current ahead of itself to depolarize the adjacent stretch of membrane; a wider axon has lower internal resistance, so current spreads farther and the spike advances faster.

The thin hair axons conduct near 0.5 m/s, and the trip from hair to connective takes about 10 ms. Part of the minimum 35 ms wind-reflex latency is therefore spent on travel in slow sensory fibers before any central relay begins.

Descending interneurons recover that time. The TCG axon is about 20 μm wide, and its stimulation evoked fictive flight after as little as 23 ms, so a wide axon carrying wind information to the thorax shortens the path from head to flight motor output.

figure.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 8. Simultaneous seta and connective recordings.

transcript: Slide 11 measures how slowly the hair axons conduct. Placing that number beside the reflex latency on slide 5 and the TCG result on slide 33 explains why a fast descending pathway matters.
Why size changes speed.
Current entering at an active patch of membrane flows along the inside of the axon, and a larger diameter offers that current less resistance.
More current reaches the membrane ahead, which reaches threshold sooner, so the spike moves forward faster.
A latency budget.
Camhi’s simultaneous recordings place about ten milliseconds between the hair tip and the connective electrode.
That delay occurs before the signal reaches any interneuron, and it is part of the overall wind-reflex delay measured on slide 5.
A fast route to the thorax.
Buhl and colleagues stimulated the large TCG axon and recorded flight onset after roughly two dozen milliseconds.
A thick descending axon moves wind information over the long distance from the head to the thoracic ganglia with little delay, so most of the remaining time is spent in central processing.
refs: J. M. Camhi (1969a). Locust wind receptors. I. Transducer mechanics and sensory response. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):335–348. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.335
J. M. Camhi (1969c). Locust wind receptors. III. Contribution to flight initiation and lift control. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):363–373. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.363

E. Buhl; K. Schildberger; P. A. Stevenson (2008). A muscarinic cholinergic mechanism underlies activation of the central pattern generator for locust flight. Journal of Experimental Biology 211(14):2346–2357. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.017384

new_slides.title: Input mix sets each interneuron’s tuning width
body: The tuning of a **convergent** interneuron, one that sums input from many receptors, depends on which receptors it collects. If its hairs prefer widely different directions, wind from almost any angle excites some of them, and the summed response stays high across a wide range of angles.

Wind-indicator cells reach about 140° this way, far wider than the roughly 54° of one hair. Wind-direction cells draw on hairs whose preferences cluster, so their summed response falls off almost as steeply as a single hair’s, near 60°.

The two designs trade one variable for another. A broad cell gives up angle but gains a reliable report that wind is present at a given strength, which suits keeping flight going. A narrow cell keeps the angle information needed to detect drift away from head-on airflow.

figure.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 3. Wind-direction tuning at several airflow speeds.

transcript: Slides 9, 12 and 13 report three tuning widths for the hair, the wind-indicator cell and the wind-direction cell. The width of an interneuron follows from how its inputs are arranged.
Summing different preferences.
When the inputs point in many directions, some are always well driven, so the total changes little as wind angle changes.
Small air jets aimed at separate hair groups revealed that a single broadly tuned cell collects from receptors on the left and right of the head pointing in many directions.
Summing similar preferences.
When the inputs share a preferred direction, they rise and fall together as the angle changes, and the sum keeps their sharpness.
Camhi’s mapping of wind-direction cells found inputs with more similar preferred directions, matching their narrower curves.
What each code is good for.
Broad pooling sacrifices angle to provide a steady intensity signal that changes little when the head turns.
Narrow tuning keeps the angle signal that a corrective steering response would need.
refs: J. M. Camhi (1969a). Locust wind receptors. I. Transducer mechanics and sensory response. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):335–348. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.335
J. M. Camhi (1969b). Locust wind receptors. II. Interneurones in the cervical connective. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):349–362. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.349

extra_figures.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 4. Spike responses to pivots of a maintained wind jet.

new_slides.title: Fast adaptation makes cells report airflow change
body: A **change detector** signals when a stimulus varies rather than its steady value. An interneuron that adapts within a fraction of a second fires briefly after a rise in its input and then falls quiet, so only fast transitions drive it strongly; a slow ramp allows adaptation to keep pace and evokes little firing.

Recentre and acceleration cells both behave this way, which accounts for short pivots and brief accelerations working best. They differ in which change they read: recentre cells need a shift in angle from one side, while acceleration cells need a rise in speed and largely ignore angle.

Change detectors can also be read faster than rate-coded cells. A cell firing steadily needs several spikes before a change in its rate stands out, whereas a quiet change detector signals with its first spike, and its first interspike interval already grades how fast the airflow changed.

figure.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 6. Responses to wind-angle shifts toward and away from center.

transcript: Slides 14 and 15 describe two rapidly adapting interneuron classes. Fast adaptation explains why both prefer quick stimuli, and their inputs explain why they read different changes.
Adaptation as a filter.
A neuron whose response declines during a maintained input passes rapid changes and suppresses steady levels.
Applied to Camhi’s cells, a pivot lasting under about one or two tenths of a second produced strong responses, while slow pivots let the response fade before it built.
Angle change versus speed change.
Recentre cells were driven by shifts toward head-on from one preferred side and largely ignored the reverse shift.
Acceleration cells responded to rising speed above a threshold near one metre per second and could ignore even sizable pivots.
Speed of readout.
Against a silent background, the first spike is itself the signal, so downstream cells need not wait to average a rate.
Camhi measured the first interspike intervals for this reason: they shortened as pivots and accelerations became faster.
refs: J. M. Camhi (1969b). Locust wind receptors. II. Interneurones in the cervical connective. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):349–362. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.349

extra_figures.caption: Camhi (1969), Fig. 8. Pivot duration versus the first interspike intervals.

new_slides.title: Deafferentation rules out a chain-reflex rhythm
body: A **chain reflex** hypothesis holds that each wing movement stimulates sense organs whose signal triggers the opposite movement, so the rhythm exists only as a loop through the periphery. A central pattern generator instead times bursts within the nervous system itself.

Each reduction removed one possible loop. Cutting wings and wing nerves removed phasic feedback, removing thoracic muscles removed any rhythm generated by contraction, and cord stimulation replaced wind with unpatterned drive. Alternation survived every step, which a chain reflex would forbid.

The reductions also measure what feedback adds. Without it the rhythm fell from about 17 to near 7 cycles/s while elevator-to-depressor delays held at 30–40 ms, so the lost time lies between successive bursts, the interval that tegula input near threshold later shortened.

figure.caption: Wilson (1961), Fig. 6. Elevator and depressor activity after severe sensory reduction.

transcript: Wilson’s experiments on slides 16 to 18 were designed against a specific alternative, the idea that flight is a chain of reflexes. Laying out that alternative explains why each reduction was informative.
The alternative being tested.
In a chain reflex, the sensory consequence of an upstroke would be the trigger for the downstroke, and the reverse.
If that were the whole mechanism, removing the sense organs or the movement would stop the rhythm.
Three independent reductions.
Wilson removed the wings and their nerves, then the muscles, and finally drove the cord electrically.
Each manipulation removed a different candidate loop, and the alternation persisted after all of them, so a central network is required.
What feedback contributes.
The intact rhythm near seventeen cycles per second dropped to around seven, yet the delay from elevator to depressor stayed similar.
Ausborn and colleagues later found that tegula stimulation near threshold sped the deafferented rhythm, consistent with feedback shortening the part of the cycle between bursts.
refs: D. M. Wilson (1961). The central nervous control of flight in a locust. Journal of Experimental Biology 38(2):471–490. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.38.2.471
J. Ausborn; W. Stein; H. Wolf (2007). Frequency control of motor patterning by negative sensory feedback. Journal of Neuroscience 27(35):9319–9328. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0907-07.2007

extra_figures.caption: Wilson (1961), Fig. 1. Published dissection identifies ganglia, nerves and muscles.

new_slides.title: 404 cells are sufficient but not always necessary
body: **Sufficiency** means that activating an element produces an outcome; **necessity** means that removing it prevents the outcome. Depolarizing one 404 neuron tests sufficiency, and hyperpolarizing it during wind tests necessity, so the two current directions answer different questions about the same cell.
One 404 cell passed the sufficiency test in quiescent preparations. The necessity test was conditional: in some preparations flight continued while current abolished every spike in the recorded cell.

That pattern fits a pool of activating neurons whose drive adds up, with the rhythm generated elsewhere. The 404 cells showed no detectable input from the rhythm generator, so the flight system is organized in levels: tonic drive from above, and cycle timing within the thoracic network.

figure.caption: Pearson et al. (1985), Fig. 9. A repeated wind pulse with and without 404 inhibition.

transcript: Slides 21 and 22 apply opposite currents to the same kind of cell. The two experiments answer two different logical questions, and the answers together define the role of the 404 group.
Two questions, two manipulations.
Adding current asks whether a cell can start flight on its own; removing its activity asks whether flight still happens without it.
A cell can pass the first test and fail the second when other neurons provide the same kind of drive.
What the 404 results give.
Pearson and colleagues found that depolarizing a single 404 neuron often started flight in a quiescent preparation.
They also found that flight sometimes persisted when all spiking in a 404 neuron was prevented, so each cell is one contributor among several.
A layered circuit.
None of their data indicated that 404 neurons receive input from the central rhythm generator.
The authors therefore described flight circuitry as hierarchical, with a tonic drive system that initiates and maintains activity in a separate patterning system.
refs: K. G. Pearson; D. N. Reye; D. W. Parsons; G. Bicker (1985). Flight-initiating interneurons in the locust. Journal of Neurophysiology 53(4):910–925. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.1985.53.4.910

extra_figures.caption: Pearson et al. (1985), Fig. 1. Filled 404 neuron in the thoracic nervous system.

new_slides.title: Resetting separates oscillator parts from followers
body: A **phase-response curve** plots how far a brief pulse shifts later cycles against the phase at which it arrives. Its logic rests on a property of oscillators: the timing of the rhythm is held in the state of its own elements, so pushing one element moves every cycle that follows.

A follower neuron behaves differently. Driving it changes its own spikes, but the oscillator keeps its schedule and the motor burst arrives on time. Resetting by 301 and 501 therefore places both cells inside the timing machinery rather than downstream of it.

The shape of each curve also points to each cell’s job. Advances and delays from 301 mean it can hasten or postpone the transition it helps start, whereas consistent delays from 501, which fires with the depressor phase and inhibits elevator pathways, fit a cell that prolongs the phase in which it is active.

figure.caption: Robertson & Pearson (1985), Fig. 1. 301 anatomy and phase-response measurements.

transcript: Slides 24 and 25 report resetting curves for two interneurons. The reasoning behind the test explains why a shifted cycle counts as evidence for rhythm generation.
What a resetting test asks.
A pulse is delivered at a chosen point in the cycle, and the arrival time of later motor bursts is compared with the expected schedule.
If the schedule shifts permanently, the pulse changed the oscillator itself.
Followers do not reset.
A motor neuron or any purely downstream cell can be driven to fire extra spikes without changing when the rhythm generator produces its following burst.
Robertson and Pearson concluded from the resetting experiments that 301 and 501 are important in rhythm generation.
Reading the cell’s role from the curve.
301 is associated with elevator activity and could both advance and delay cycles.
501 bursts with the depressor phase and inhibits elevator-related cells, so extra excitation of 501 lengthens the depressor phase and delays the cycle.
refs: R. M. Robertson; K. G. Pearson (1985). Neural circuits in the flight system of the locust. Journal of Neurophysiology 53(1):110–128. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.1985.53.1.110

new_slides.title: Disinhibition reverses at the IPSP reversal point
body: A **reversal potential** is the membrane voltage at which a channel’s net current is zero; on either side the current flows in opposite directions. Chloride-dependent inhibition usually reverses below rest, so opening those channels pulls the membrane down.

If 501 receives tonic inhibition, part of its resting state is a steady inhibitory current. A 301 spike that briefly silences the inhibiting neuron removes that current, and 501 depolarizes. Holding 501 below the inhibitory reversal potential flips the steady current’s direction, so removing it hyperpolarizes the cell instead.

Chloride loading raises the reversal potential and shrinks the steady inhibition, leaving less to remove. Picrotoxin blocks it outright, so 501 depolarized and the delayed potential vanished. All three tests converge on one step: an inhibitory synapse acting on another inhibitory neuron.

figure.caption: Robertson & Pearson (1985), Fig. 6. Delayed potentials reverse during hyperpolarizing current injection.

transcript: Slides 27 and 28 report three tests of the delayed potential in 501. Each result follows from what a reversal potential is, applied to a response produced by removing inhibition.
Driving force.
The current through a channel depends on how far the membrane sits from that channel’s reversal potential.
At the reversal potential an open inhibitory channel passes no net current, and beyond it the current reverses.
Why a removal response reverses.
A depolarization caused by losing inhibition is the mirror image of that inhibition.

When current pushes 501 past the inhibitory reversal point, the tonic current changes direction, and its removal changes direction with it, which matches the spontaneous inhibitory potentials reversing at a similar level.
Two further manipulations.
Loading the cell with chloride moves the reversal potential toward rest, so the tonic inhibition is weaker and its removal has less effect.
Picrotoxin removes the inhibition entirely, so 501 is left depolarized and nothing remains for a 301 spike to take away.
refs: R. M. Robertson; K. G. Pearson (1985). Neural circuits in the flight system of the locust. Journal of Neurophysiology 53(1):110–128. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.1985.53.1.110

extra_figures.caption: Robertson & Pearson (1985), Fig. 7. Recorded inhibitory links through interneuron 511.

new_slides.title: A brief command can launch seconds of flight
body: Acetylcholine acts through two receptor classes with different time courses. A **nicotinic** receptor is itself a channel and opens within milliseconds while transmitter is bound; a **muscarinic** receptor activates G proteins that alter other channels through intracellular steps, so its effects build and decay more slowly.

A slow, outlasting effect suits flight activation. A train of 20 TCG pulses, over in a fraction of a second, evoked several seconds of fictive flight, so the command leaves an excited network state that persists after its own spikes stop, and atropine sensitivity places that state at muscarinic receptors.

The same timing distinction fits the drug results. Nicotine’s brief, uncoordinated burst resembles a fast channel response that subsides quickly, whereas muscarinic agonists produced stable alternation that persisted while the network supplied the rhythm.

figure.caption: Buhl et al. (2008), Fig. 4. TCG stimulation, atropine blockade and wash recovery.

transcript: Slides 30, 31 and 33 identify a muscarinic step in flight activation. The time course of muscarinic signaling helps explain why a short burst of command activity can be followed by a long flight episode.
Two receptor classes.
Ionotropic receptors such as the nicotinic type open a pore directly, so their current tracks the presence of transmitter closely.
Metabotropic receptors such as the muscarinic type act through G proteins and second messengers, and their effects can last well beyond the transmitter pulse.
A short command and a long episode.
The TCG stimulus lasted only as long as twenty pulses at two hundred per second, yet flight continued for seconds.
That persistence is consistent with a slow excitatory state in the flight network, and Buhl and colleagues found that atropine blocked the response reversibly.
Matching the drug responses.
Nicotine gave a short burst of uncoordinated motor activity, as expected from fast direct excitation without recruitment of the generator.
Muscarinic agonists instead produced sustained flight, with the cycle-by-cycle timing coming from the network’s own synaptic interactions.
refs: E. Buhl; K. Schildberger; P. A. Stevenson (2008). A muscarinic cholinergic mechanism underlies activation of the central pattern generator for locust flight. Journal of Experimental Biology 211(14):2346–2357. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.017384

new_slides.title: Three drug tests separate activation from modulation
body: Pharmacology answers different questions depending on the test. An **agonist** asks whether stimulating a receptor can produce flight, an **antagonist** asks whether natural activation passes through that receptor, and **depletion** asks whether the transmitter itself must be present.

Amines passed only the first test: octopamine, tyramine, dopamine and histamine released flight in the bath, yet aminergic antagonists did not reversibly block wind-induced flight, and reserpine-treated locusts still flew. Muscarinic signaling passed the second test for wind, pilocarpine, amines and TCG alike.

Relying on agonists alone would have named octopamine the flight trigger. The combined results give amines a modulatory role, raising wind effectiveness and tightening leg-wing coupling at lower doses, and give acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors the activating role.

figure.caption: Buhl et al. (2008), Fig. 6. Octopamine staining and flight output after reserpine.

new_slides.cite: Buhl et al. (2008); Rillich et al. (2013)
transcript: Slides 30 to 35 use agonists, antagonists and depletion on the same flight preparation. The three methods test different claims, and only their combination assigns roles to acetylcholine and the amines.
What each test can show.
An agonist establishes only that a receptor can drive the circuit when flooded with drug, which says nothing about whether natural activation uses it.
An antagonist tests whether natural activation passes through the receptor, and depletion tests whether the endogenous transmitter must be available.
How the two transmitter systems scored.
Buhl and colleagues found that several amines started flight in the bath, but aminergic antagonists did not reversibly block initiation and amine-depleted animals still flew to wind.
Atropine and scopolamine, in contrast, reversibly blocked flight evoked by wind, cholinergic agonists, octopamine and TCG stimulation.
A modulatory role for amines.
Rillich and colleagues found that a lower octopamine dose raised the probability that wind released flight and tightened coupling between leg and wing units.
Earlier work had credited octopamine with activating the flight generator; the combined tests move that role to acetylcholine acting at muscarinic receptors.
refs: E. Buhl; K. Schildberger; P. A. Stevenson (2008). A muscarinic cholinergic mechanism underlies activation of the central pattern generator for locust flight. Journal of Experimental Biology 211(14):2346–2357. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.017384

J. Rillich; P. A. Stevenson; H.-J. Pflueger (2013). Flight and walking in locusts–cholinergic co-activation, temporal coupling and its modulation by biogenic amines. PLOS ONE 8(5):e62899. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0062899

new_slides.title: Stronger negative feedback lengthens each cycle
body: **Negative feedback** is a loop in which an output generates a signal that opposes further change in that output. The tegula fires during the downstroke, and its input pushes the network toward elevation, ending the phase that produced it.

Weak feedback arriving at the right moment hastens the switch to elevation, which shortens the cycle and raises frequency. Stronger trains last longer and recruit more afferents, so their excitation spills into the following phase, where inhibition within the network holds off the depressor motor neurons longer.

Each stimulus train was timed from the depressor burst, so a later depressor burst also postpones the following feedback and carries the delay into every later cycle. The loop therefore settles at lower frequencies as feedback strength rises, a property expected of negative feedback in general.

figure.caption: Ausborn et al. (2007), Fig. 2(A). Wing motion and elevator recordings during tegula stimulation.

transcript: Slides 37 to 39 move from open-loop resetting to closed-loop control of frequency. The concept of negative feedback explains how one sensory loop can both speed and slow the rhythm.
The loop.
Wing depression activates the tegula, and the tegula signal promotes the switch to elevation.
Ausborn and colleagues describe this as negative feedback, since the sensory signal opposes continuation of the movement that caused it.
Weak versus strong feedback.
A small, well-timed input advances the transition and so shortens each cycle, which is why frequency rose near threshold.
With more afferents recruited and longer trains, excitation reaches parts of the network whose inhibitory actions postpone the downstroke burst.
Why the effect accumulates.
In closed loop, the timing of each stimulus depends on the preceding depressor burst, so a delay is passed on from cycle to cycle.

The authors found the same relation in their model and in the animal: stronger tegula feedback gave lower cycle frequency, and they suggest this is a general emergent property of negative feedback systems.
refs: J. Ausborn; W. Stein; H. Wolf (2007). Frequency control of motor patterning by negative sensory feedback. Journal of Neuroscience 27(35):9319–9328. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0907-07.2007

extra_figures.caption: Ausborn et al. (2007), Fig. 1(A). Published ganglion and tegula-nerve recording preparation.

new_slides.title: Walking and flight are chosen upstream of their CPGs
body: Two behaviors can be mutually exclusive for two different reasons. Their pattern generators might inhibit each other, so that one running silences the other, or the generators might be independent and the choice made by which activating inputs reach them.

Co-activation in the deafferented locust favors the second explanation. A shared or mutually inhibitory kernel would force the two patterns to alternate, yet slow stepping and fast wing alternation ran side by side.

Selection must then occur in the pathways removed by deafferentation. Tarsal contact, which holds flight off in a standing locust, is one such pathway, and releasing stimuli such as head wind supply another, so the intact animal recruits one program by gating its activation.

figure.caption: Rillich et al. (2013), Fig. 3(A). Simultaneous leg and wing output during pilocarpine exposure.

transcript: Slides 40 and 41 find walking and flight patterns running at the same time in one reduced nervous system. Comparing two ways of keeping behaviors exclusive explains what that finding implies for the intact animal.
Two candidate mechanisms.
If the generators inhibited each other, activating one would suppress the other, and the patterns would alternate rather than overlap.
If the generators are independent, exclusivity has to come from the inputs that switch each one on.
The co-activation test.
Rillich and colleagues saw no sign of mutual inhibition, such as alternating sequences of the two patterns, and the walking rhythm did not change when flight began.
They conclude that the activation pathways and core circuits of the two generators are functionally and anatomically separate.
Selection in the intact locust.
The authors point to sensory mechanisms such as the tarsal reflex, together with natural releasing stimuli, as the means of selecting one behavior.
Camhi’s finding that foot contact can inhibit flight on slide 6 is one such mechanism, and deafferentation removes it.
refs: J. Rillich; P. A. Stevenson; H.-J. Pflueger (2013). Flight and walking in locusts–cholinergic co-activation, temporal coupling and its modulation by biogenic amines. PLOS ONE 8(5):e62899. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0062899
J. M. Camhi (1969c). Locust wind receptors. III. Contribution to flight initiation and lift control. Journal of Experimental Biology 50(2):363–373. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.50.2.363

extra_figures.caption: Rillich et al. (2013), Fig. 4. Drug concentration changes the expressed leg and wing motor patterns.

new_slides.title: DUM neurons prime glycolysis before take-off
body: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activates phosphofructokinase, a rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, so raising it speeds carbohydrate breakdown in muscle. The DUM pathway reaches it in steps: octopamine binds muscle receptors, cAMP rises, PKA phosphorylates target proteins, and the regulator’s level climbs.

Timing makes this control useful. DUM neurons supplying flight muscle are active at rest but selectively inhibited during flight, so octopamine primes the muscle for the high carbohydrate demand of take-off and then declines once flight is under way.

Falling glycolytic activation during prolonged flight fits the locust’s shift toward lipid as its main fuel, which spares limited carbohydrate reserves on long flights. Central neurons thus set the muscle’s fuel choice according to behavioral state, while motor neurons drive contraction.

figure.caption: Mentel et al. (2003), Fig. 3. PKA blockade and cAMP-donor effects on the glycolytic regulator.

transcript: Slides 43 and 44 show DUM stimulation raising a glycolytic regulator through PKA. The enzyme it acts on and the timing of DUM activity explain what this does for a flying locust.
From neuron to enzyme.
Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase, which controls flux through glycolysis.
Mentel and colleagues found that PKA is necessary for the DUM effect, placing a cAMP-dependent step between octopamine release and the rise in the regulator.
Active at rest, silent in flight.
According to the authors, DUM neurons innervating the flight muscles fire during rest and are selectively inhibited during flight.
The muscle is therefore poised for carbohydrate use when flight begins, and that stimulation fades as flight continues.
Fuel switching.
Take-off requires high rates of carbohydrate oxidation, but locusts soon switch to lipid on long flights to spare limited carbohydrate.
Removing the octopaminergic drive during flight tends to lower muscle glycolysis, which fits that switch.
refs: T. Mentel; C. Duch; H. Stypa; G. Wegener; U. Müller; H.-J. Pflüger (2003). Central modulatory neurons control fuel selection in flight muscle of migratory locust. Journal of Neuroscience 23(4):1109–1113. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-04-01109.2003

extra_figures.caption: Mentel et al. (2003), Fig. 1. DUM projections and the controlled flight-muscle preparation.

original_edits.old: These relationships define an organized motor pattern rather than undifferentiated muscle excitation. Later deafferented preparations retained alternation and a hindwing lead, but their measured delays depended on the experimental treatment. Intact movement timing and reduced-preparation muscle timing are related measurements with different mechanical conditions.
original_edits.new: These relationships define an organized motor pattern rather than undifferentiated muscle excitation. Later deafferented preparations retained alternation and a hindwing lead, so both features arise within the thoracic circuitry. Left and right homologous muscles also fired nearly synchronously there, preserving the bilateral coordination of the intact motor score.

original_edits.old: Directing wind at the wing instead of the head did not reproduce the response. This control supports a sensory-mediated adjustment rather than a direct aerodynamic twisting effect. The head-wind experiment measured wing angle, so the corresponding change in lift remained a functional interpretation rather than a simultaneous force measurement.
original_edits.new: Directing wind at the wing instead of the head did not reproduce the response. This control supports a sensory-mediated adjustment rather than a direct aerodynamic twisting effect. After a wind acceleration, an added reduction in pronation appeared within about 80 ms, so head receptors adjust each downstroke within a few wingbeats.

original_edits.old: Covering the head hairs prevented wind-triggered opening; removing the covering restored it. The hairs therefore supplied the tested reflex pathway. The latency difference supports an additional jump-associated initiating pathway, while the behavioral experiment alone does not identify its neurons.
original_edits.new: Covering the head hairs prevented wind-triggered opening; removing the covering restored it. The hairs therefore supplied the tested reflex pathway. Jump-associated wing opening, beginning well before the fastest wind response, depends on a faster initiating route than the hair reflex.

original_edits.old: Loss of contact can therefore release flight under these conditions, but its latency is longer than jump-associated wing opening. The controls reduce explanations based on shock to the tether or insufficient initial contact. They do not identify the central pathway that couples jumping to flying.
original_edits.new: Loss of contact can therefore release flight under these conditions, but its latency is longer than jump-associated wing opening. The controls reduce explanations based on shock to the tether or insufficient initial contact. Similar latencies with one leg or several legs place the delay in the central response.

original_edits.old: Different preferred directions allow the head to distribute airflow information across receptors. A single receptor’s firing rate still depends on both wind direction and speed, so it is not an unambiguous speed meter. The anatomical map predicts preferred direction but does not measure the full response of every smaller hair.
original_edits.new: Different preferred directions allow the head to distribute airflow information across receptors. A single receptor’s firing rate still depends on both wind direction and speed, so it is not an unambiguous speed meter. Similar maps across animals mean that a given hair position reports a similar wind angle in every locust.

original_edits.old: The sensory discharge contains both an onset response and information about continuing airflow. Adaptation does not imply complete loss of sensitivity. Because these recordings were extracellular, they establish action-potential timing but do not directly measure the receptor current or identify its mechanically gated ion channel.
original_edits.new: The sensory discharge contains both an onset response and information about continuing airflow. A receptor still firing near 125 spikes/s after adapting keeps reporting head wind for as long as the airflow lasts, which in a flying locust means throughout the flight.

original_edits.old: The rate therefore combines direction and speed rather than representing either variable alone. The alignment of response and shaft curvature links anatomy to sensory tuning. These measurements do not establish the decoding operation performed by downstream interneurons or behaviorally achievable angular precision.
original_edits.new: The rate therefore combines direction and speed rather than representing either variable alone. The alignment of response and shaft curvature links anatomy to sensory tuning. Faster wind raised firing at every angle, so speed scales the whole tuning curve while the hair’s curvature fixes where its peak lies.

original_edits.old: No tested component alone accounted for the narrow wind-tuning curve. The results support combined contributions from mechanical structure and sensory coupling. They do not identify the molecular transduction channel, and the remounted-shaft experiment depended on the mechanical properties of the replacement socket.
original_edits.new: No tested component alone accounted for the narrow wind-tuning curve. The results support combined contributions from mechanical structure and sensory coupling. Each asymmetry favors displacement in one plane, so their effects add, and the intact hair ends up more selective than any single mechanism makes it.

original_edits.old: These tests support axons passing through the brain and terminating before the thoracic pathway, probably in the suboesophageal ganglion. The physiological inference is stronger than visual proximity alone. It does not reconstruct every terminal branch or directly identify each sensory-to-interneuron synapse.
original_edits.new: These tests support axons passing through the brain and terminating before the thoracic pathway, probably in the suboesophageal ganglion. Wind information therefore reaches thoracic flight circuits only after a synaptic relay to interneurons that descend in the cervical connective.

original_edits.old: Pooling differently tuned receptors is consistent with a broad signal for the presence and intensity of airflow. The recordings and receptive-field tests do not directly establish the exact synaptic weights. Camhi’s classification described response properties rather than assigning each unit a modern identified-cell label.
original_edits.new: Pooling differently tuned receptors is consistent with a broad signal for the presence and intensity of airflow. Single-hair deflection rarely evoked interneuron spikes, while stimulating separate hair groups together preserved or increased the response, so each cell sums excitation from many receptors.

original_edits.old: A downstream cell can therefore emphasize directional information while remaining sensitive to stimulus strength and change. These findings support a possible role in directional stabilization, but Camhi did not prove that a particular recorded unit was necessary for a specific yaw-correction movement.
original_edits.new: A downstream cell can therefore emphasize directional information while remaining sensitive to stimulus strength and change. The extra burst when wind swings toward the preferred side suits a signal for yaw, the rotation about the vertical axis that changes head-wind angle in flight.

original_edits.old: The response distinguishes the direction of a change, beyond the starting and ending wind angles alone. The preparation establishes temporal and directional selectivity. A role in terminating corrective turns was proposed from these properties, but not verified by selective cell manipulation.
original_edits.new: The response distinguishes the direction of a change, beyond the starting and ending wind angles alone. The preparation establishes temporal and directional selectivity. Rapid shifts of this kind accompany sudden body turns in flight, when the head-wind angle changes within a fraction of a second.

original_edits.old: Their response therefore differs from both sustained wind-indication and directional recentring. It is consistent with a transient signal about airflow onset. The recordings do not establish that acceleration cells alone initiate flight, especially because free-jump wing opening occurs faster than the tested wind reflex.
original_edits.new: Their response therefore differs from both sustained wind-indication and directional recentring. It is consistent with a transient signal about airflow onset. Wind accelerations of 100–600 m/s² released flight in the reflex tests, so the stimuli that start flight are those that drive these cells most strongly.

original_edits.old: Wing movement and its feedback were therefore unnecessary for the basic alternation. This does not mean that feedback is unnecessary for normal frequency, aerodynamic control or stable free flight. Continuous sensory excitation from the head supplied activation without specifying every phase of the rhythm.
original_edits.new: Wing movement and its feedback were therefore unnecessary for the basic alternation. The thoracic ganglia hold a network whose own connections time elevator and depressor bursts, and identified interneurons such as 301 and 501 belong to it. Continuous sensory excitation from the head supplied activation.

original_edits.old: Rhythm without attached flight muscles excludes a muscle-driven reflex chain as the sole origin of the recorded bursts. The reduced output still differed from intact flight. Preparation damage and lost feedback limit conclusions about the normal precision and contributions of each segment.
original_edits.new: Rhythm without attached flight muscles excludes a muscle-driven reflex chain as the sole origin of the recorded bursts. An orderly metathoracic rhythm beside an irregular mesothoracic one suggests that each segment’s circuitry can oscillate partly on its own, with intersegmental coupling holding them in step.

original_edits.old: Central circuitry can therefore transform continuing excitation into patterned alternation. This experiment does not require a single dedicated pacemaker neuron. Electrical cord stimulation recruits multiple axons, so it cannot identify the natural activating cell or its transmitter.
original_edits.new: Central circuitry can therefore transform continuing excitation into patterned alternation, arising from network interactions rather than one dedicated pacemaker neuron. Natural activation works the same way: tonic wind drive and steady 404 discharge release a rhythm whose frequency the circuit sets.

original_edits.old: This separates an activating pathway from neurons that determine successive phases. The small 404 group contains physiological and anatomical variation, so results from one member do not imply identical sensory input to every member. Tonic activity supplies drive rather than a complete motor score.
original_edits.new: This separates an activating pathway from neurons that determine successive phases. Darkness and wind both raised 404 firing, so visual and mechanosensory triggers for flight converge on the same thoracic cells. Tonic activity supplies drive rather than a complete motor score.

original_edits.old: The association is consistent with an excitatory drive that regulates circuit activation. Correlation alone does not prove that 404 firing causes the frequency change, because both could respond to another input. Current-injection experiments supplied the additional causal test.
original_edits.new: The association is consistent with an excitatory drive that regulates circuit activation. A linear relation between discharge rate and flight frequency allows the network to read 404 drive as a graded speed command, and injected current confirmed the causal direction.

original_edits.old: This is causal evidence that one 404 neuron can recruit the central flight program. It establishes sufficiency in favorable preparations, not that the cell acts alone in the intact animal. Wind normally activates several pathways, whereas current injection selectively increases one neuron’s drive.
original_edits.new: This is causal evidence that one 404 neuron can recruit the central flight program. A steady, unpatterned depolarization of one cell produced rhythmic alternation, so the timing of each cycle comes from the network it drives, as with Wilson’s cord stimulation.

original_edits.old: A single member of the activating group can therefore influence whether the circuit reaches its activation threshold. The condition dependence prevents interpreting this as universal necessity of one cell. Other 404 neurons and parallel inputs can contribute enough drive under stronger stimulation.
original_edits.new: A single member of the activating group can therefore influence whether the circuit reaches its activation threshold. Hyperpolarizing a 404 neuron during an ongoing episode also slowed or stopped the rhythm, matching the link between 404 firing rate and flight frequency.

original_edits.old: The temporal relationship and the ability of 404 stimulation to release flight support a possible central link between jump-related activity and flight initiation. The source of the kick-associated excitation was unresolved. These recordings were not direct proof that 404 neurons trigger wing opening during natural jumps.
original_edits.new: The temporal relationship and the ability of 404 stimulation to release flight support a possible central link between jump-related activity and flight initiation. A 404 burst just before take-off is a candidate route for wing opening within about 15 ms of jump onset, well ahead of the fastest wind reflex.

original_edits.old: Phase-dependent resetting supplies causal evidence for participation in rhythm generation. It does not prove that 301 is the sole oscillator or that the tested pulse reproduces its natural synaptic input. The response must be interpreted within the connected flight network.
original_edits.new: Phase-dependent resetting supplies causal evidence for participation in rhythm generation. 301 fires with elevator-related activity, and its branches in two thoracic ganglia suit it to coordinate forewing and hindwing circuits within one rhythm.

original_edits.old: The distinction between 301 and 501 argues against treating every rhythmically active interneuron as functionally interchangeable. 501 can alter when the network moves into its next cycle. Current injection establishes a network effect while leaving other neurons and parallel oscillatory mechanisms available.
original_edits.new: The distinction between 301 and 501 argues against treating every rhythmically active interneuron as functionally interchangeable. 501 can alter when the network moves into its following cycle. It also inhibits 301 within about 3 ms, so the two resetting cells are directly connected.

original_edits.old: These paired recordings establish directional physiological interactions. A longer latency suggests additional processing but does not alone count synapses. The 301-to-501 depolarization required further tests because depolarization can arise from removal of inhibition rather than direct excitatory transmitter action.
original_edits.new: These paired recordings establish directional physiological interactions. Each 301 spike excites 501 after a delay, and each 501 spike quickly inhibits 301, so 301 activity recruits the cell that ends it. Such a reciprocal pair is a circuit motif suited to promoting rhythmic bursting.

original_edits.old: An identified pathway through interneuron 511 contained inhibition from 301 to 511 and from 511 to 501. The observations support delayed excitation through disinhibition, but tonic graded transmitter release at the candidate intermediate connection was not directly established.
original_edits.new: An identified pathway through interneuron 511 contained inhibition from 301 to 511 and from 511 to 501. In the authors’ interpretation, 301 inhibits graded, tonic transmitter release from intercalated neurons, so the delayed excitation travels a disynaptic route.

original_edits.old: Blocking an inhibitory influence can remove a depolarizing response that depends on disinhibition. The result supports that mechanism but does not identify a particular inhibitory transmitter or receptor subunit. Persistent, distorted rhythmicity also argues against assigning all oscillation to this one interaction.
original_edits.new: Blocking an inhibitory influence can remove a depolarizing response that depends on disinhibition. The faster rhythm with disrupted phases that persisted under picrotoxin indicates that inhibitory connections set both cycle timing and phase, while other oscillatory mechanisms survive the block.

original_edits.old: The chain supplies a physiological route by which central activity can establish phase relationships in motor output. It is part of a broader network, with additional excitation and inhibition. The recorded connections do not establish that the chain is the only route to every depressor motor neuron.
original_edits.new: The chain supplies a physiological route by which central activity can establish phase relationships in motor output. Two delayed stages between 301 activity and depressor drive account for the constant latency between elevator and depressor depolarizations and the steady depressor burst duration.

original_edits.old: The agonist establishes that muscarinic stimulation can recruit the flight circuitry without phasic wing feedback. Bath sufficiency does not identify the endogenous releasing neuron, local transmitter concentration, or receptor subtype. The retained muscle arrangement and phase relationships distinguish a flight score from general hyperactivity.
original_edits.new: The agonist establishes that muscarinic stimulation can recruit the flight circuitry without phasic wing feedback. Eserine, which blocks acetylcholinesterase and so prolongs the action of the animal’s own acetylcholine, also initiated fictive flight. The retained muscle arrangement and phase relationships distinguish a flight score from general hyperactivity.

original_edits.old: Direct excitation of motor activity is therefore insufficient evidence for CPG recruitment. Combined muscarinic and nicotinic actions may support faster output, but the experiment did not isolate every cellular contribution. The nicotinic antagonist tests were not selectively reversible at doses that abolished activity.
original_edits.new: Brief, uncoordinated motor activity under nicotine marks direct excitation of motor pathways, whereas a stable alternating score marks CPG recruitment. Carbachol’s faster rhythm compared with pilocarpine fits combined muscarinic and nicotinic actions adding drive to a circuit already recruited through muscarinic receptors.

original_edits.old: Reversibility reduces an explanation based solely on irreversible tissue damage. Blockade of natural stimulation and an agonist supports a necessary muscarinic step in the tested pathway. High bath doses and the absence of cell-specific receptor manipulation limit assignment of the affected receptor to a particular interneuron.
original_edits.new: Reversibility reduces an explanation based solely on irreversible tissue damage. Blockade of natural stimulation and an agonist supports a necessary muscarinic step in the tested pathway. Agreement between two structurally different antagonists ties the block to the receptor class they share.

original_edits.old: The short latency and reversible block support a muscarinic step close to the flight-generating circuit. They do not prove that TCG itself releases acetylcholine: its follower neuron could supply the cholinergic action. The experiment established a receptor-dependent route from an identified activating neuron to motor output.
original_edits.new: The short latency and reversible block support a muscarinic step close to the flight-generating circuit. TCG, or the follower cell it excites inside the flight-generating circuit, is therefore likely cholinergic. The experiment established a receptor-dependent route from an identified activating neuron to motor output.

original_edits.old: Drug-induced sufficiency does not establish an amine as the indispensable natural trigger. The antagonist result places muscarinic action downstream of, or within, the amine-recruited activation route. Bath drug potency cannot be equated with natural release probability or concentration at receptors behind the insect blood–brain barrier.
original_edits.new: The antagonist result places muscarinic action downstream of, or within, the amine-recruited activation route. A flight network that responds to so many amines fits a system in which several modulators can raise excitability, while the activating step itself remains cholinergic.

original_edits.old: The verified loss of labeling strengthens the conclusion that normal amine stores are not required for initiation in this preparation. It does not prove that amines never affect intact flight, or exclude every residual molecule. Muscarinic activation remains distinguishable from aminergic facilitation and motor-pattern tuning.
original_edits.new: The verified loss of labeling strengthens the conclusion that normal amine stores are not required for initiation in this preparation. Reserpine also emptied the DUM neurons supplying the flight neuropil, the only identified candidates for aminergic modulation of the flight circuit.

original_edits.old: Similar alternating patterns therefore need not have identical temporal structure. The chemistry used to release a motor program can also tune the program. These values describe deafferented preparations and should not be treated as interchangeable with the frequency, forces or wing angles of intact flight.
original_edits.new: Similar alternating patterns therefore need not have identical temporal structure. The chemistry used to release a motor program can also tune the program. Octopamine moved elevator activity later in the cycle, so an aminergic state can change how each wingbeat is divided between downstroke and upstroke.

original_edits.old: The tegula can therefore reset a centrally generated rhythm instead of merely reporting its movement. The response depends on circuit state and effective sensory input. Electrical activation substitutes for natural hair movement, so it does not reproduce every mechanical detail of the intact wing-base receptor.
original_edits.new: The tegula can therefore reset a centrally generated rhythm instead of merely reporting its movement. The response depends on circuit state and effective sensory input. Signaling each downstroke, the tegula excites elevator motor neurons and so triggers the upstroke at a time tied to actual wing position.

original_edits.old: Stimulus strength is therefore an experimentally controlled way to change the sensory drive reaching the network. It is not a direct measurement of natural synaptic gain at one identified receptor connection. The resulting network response must also be assessed with feedback timing allowed to depend on motor output.
original_edits.new: Stimulus strength is therefore an experimentally controlled way to change the sensory drive reaching the network. Larger stimuli recruit more afferents, mimicking a stronger natural signal from more tegula receptors, and in closed loop that strength can be varied while timing stays locked to each depressor burst.

original_edits.old: Stronger sensory excitation does not therefore guarantee a faster closed-loop rhythm. Timing, stimulus duration and network inhibition interact across cycles. The experimental recordings confirm a feedback-dependent relationship predicted by a model, but they do not establish every ionic current assumed by that model.
original_edits.new: Stronger sensory excitation does not therefore guarantee a faster closed-loop rhythm. Timing, stimulus duration and network inhibition interact across cycles. A computational model of the flight system predicted this relation, and feedback strength set cycle frequency in both the model and the animal.

original_edits.old: The two CPGs can therefore remain active concurrently in a reduced nervous system. This does not mean that intact locusts normally walk and fly simultaneously. Behavioral exclusivity can depend on additional selection mechanisms rather than obligatory inhibition between the core rhythm generators.
original_edits.new: The two CPGs can therefore remain active concurrently in a reduced nervous system. Walking usually started first, and its swing-stance rhythm kept its basic timing after flight began. The flight circuit thus influences leg output, whereas walking left the flight rhythm unchanged.

original_edits.old: The effect of an amine therefore includes which motor state becomes available and how outputs are coordinated. Structural relatedness does not imply interchangeable physiological action. The experiment establishes responses to applied drugs rather than the timing of natural octopamine or tyramine release during flight choice.
original_edits.new: The effect of an amine therefore includes which motor state becomes available and how outputs are coordinated. Tyramine favors walking and octopamine favors flight with leg units recruited into the flight score, consistent with the two amines acting as independent signals through dedicated receptors.

original_edits.old: These observations support octopaminergic modulation of recruitment and coordination. They do not contradict the persistence of initiation after amine depletion: facilitation and obligatory activation are different causal roles. The experiment did not directly localize the receptor responsible for coupling to a single CPG neuron.
original_edits.new: These observations support octopaminergic modulation of recruitment and coordination. Facilitation and obligatory activation are different causal roles, so octopamine can raise wind effectiveness although amine-depleted locusts still initiate flight. Tighter coupling of a stance-phase leg unit to wingbeats may help steer or stabilize flight.

original_edits.old: Central modulatory neurons can therefore prepare the muscle’s metabolic state without themselves generating wingbeat contractions. The within-animal comparison supports a peripheral effect of DUM activity. It does not establish that these neurons initiate the flight CPG or remain equally active throughout sustained flight.
original_edits.new: Central modulatory neurons can therefore prepare the muscle’s metabolic state without themselves generating wingbeat contractions. The within-animal comparison supports a peripheral effect of DUM activity. Octopamine released from DUM terminals carries the signal, linking an amine that modulates central flight circuits to the muscle’s energy supply.

original_edits.old: PKA signaling is therefore necessary under these test conditions but is insufficient by itself for the metabolic response. A parallel pathway, possibly involving calcium signaling, was proposed but not established. The experiment concerns muscle metabolism, and cannot be transferred directly to muscarinic activation of thoracic CPG neurons.
original_edits.new: PKA signaling is therefore necessary but not sufficient for the metabolic response, pointing to a second, parallel pathway, possibly calcium-dependent. Octopamine released by DUM neurons can thus act through more than one intracellular route to raise carbohydrate use in flight muscle.

original_edits.old: A CPG is therefore part of a sensorimotor system rather than a guarantee of normal movement in isolation. Central drive, synaptic network interactions, receptor-dependent state and reciprocal feedback contribute different functions. The cited preparations establish those distinctions without providing a complete reconstruction of every connection required for intact flight.
original_edits.new: A CPG is therefore part of a sensorimotor system rather than a guarantee of normal movement in isolation. Wind hairs and 404 cells activate the network, muscarinic signaling sets its activated state, inhibitory interneuron loops pattern each cycle, and tegula feedback adjusts its frequency to the wing’s actual motion.
